turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome in. My name is Dr. Lee — I'll be talking with you today. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: I came in because I spend far too much of the day checking things. I keep opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes to make sure my important papers and keepsakes are still where I left them—even if I checked them just a few minutes ago.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient reports repeatedly checking folders, drawers, and labeled boxes for reassurance even minutes after checking, consistent with repetitive checking compulsions.

turns.doctor_question: When you're checking these things repeatedly, does it feel like an unwanted urge that bothers you and that you wish you could stop, or does it feel like the right and necessary thing to do to keep things in order?
turns.patient_response: It feels like something I have to do, even though I know I just looked. I keep reopening the folders and drawers, checking the boxes again, and it takes up far too much of my day.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes repeated checking of folders, drawers, and boxes as something they feel compelled to do despite knowing they have just checked, and reports that it consumes much of the day.

turns.doctor_question: When you go back to check, is it because you have a nagging thought or fear that something bad might have happened if you don't check, or is it because you honestly can't remember whether you already checked?
turns.patient_response: It’s more the nagging thought. I’ll think, “What if I threw away my husband’s old tax papers?” or put one of the family recipes in the wrong box. Even though I know that’s probably not true, I feel terribly careless until I go back and check.

symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient describes recurrent nagging 'what if' thoughts that persist despite recognizing they are probably untrue and drive checking behavior.

turns.doctor_question: Do these checking urges and the thoughts behind them cause you significant distress or take up a lot of your time each day, or would you say they're just one part of a broader pattern of worrying about many different areas of your life?
turns.patient_response: It takes up a great deal of time. I’ve had to cancel mentoring sessions and miss book club because I lose whole afternoons checking. Then I’m embarrassed to have anyone over when the apartment is still in disarray.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient reports losing whole afternoons to checking, indicating time-consuming repetitive checking behavior with significant functional impact.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from checking on your papers and keepsakes, do you find it very difficult to throw away or get rid of items you no longer need, even ones of little practical value?
turns.patient_response: I’m not sure that’s the issue, really. I do hang onto some things, but I haven’t particularly noticed that I can’t get rid of things I don’t need.

turns.doctor_question: When you feel the urge to go back and check, do you ever try to resist it or stop yourself from checking, even if it's hard to do so?
turns.patient_response: I do try to tell myself not to, especially when I’ve only checked a few minutes earlier. But I get so uneasy that I usually end up opening the folders and drawers again anyway, just to make sure everything is still where I left it.

symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes attempting to resist repetitive checking but usually reopening folders and drawers due to unease, consistent with compulsive checking behavior.
